Topic
First law of thermodynamics — the four canonical quasistatic processes on an ideal gas.

Four quasistatic paths of an ideal gas, with the first-law ledger beside the PV diagram.

Reading a PV diagram; matching each constraint to its path; watching Q, W and ΔU close.

Guided Inquiry

The first law, three terms

Every process obeys ΔU = Q − W: change in internal energy equals heat absorbed by the gas minus work the gas does on its surroundings. Watch the ledger on the sidebar as you sweep the volume slider. The question this simulation asks: for each of the four processes, which term is zero, and why?

Predict: adiabatic expansion

The cylinder is now insulated — no heat can cross the boundary. You push the piston out, and the gas expands. Which of the three terms is zero?

Observe: run the adiabatic

Pick Adiabatic above and drag the volume slider from 10 L outward. The ledger strikes out Q. Temperature falls (the piston shading cools). The path on the PV diagram is steeper than the isotherm dashed behind it — that steeper slope is γ > 1 in PVγ = const.

Predict: isothermal expansion

Now reconnect the reservoir at 300 K. As the gas expands, its temperature is held fixed. Which term is zero?

The other two — and one misconception

Isobaric (constant pressure): none of the three vanishes — heat in, work out, and T changes. Isochoric (constant volume): the piston cannot move, so W = 0 and every joule of heat becomes internal energy.

So "expanding gas always cools" and "adding heat always does work" are both false. The isotherm expands with no cooling; the isochoric heat does no work. Which term vanishes is decided entirely by what you hold fixed.

01

At a glance

A gas in a cylinder is taken from one state to another along four different paths. Each path holds one thing fixed, and the sim keeps a running ledger of the energy that goes in, comes out and stays behind.

What you'll learn

  • How the first law ΔU = Q − W balances the energy of a gas.
  • How to read work as the area under a path on a PV diagram.
  • Which of ΔU, Q and W is pinned to zero on each of the four paths, and why.
The gas, the piston that moves, and a reservoir that can supply or take heat.

  • Cylinder (left): the gas, the piston and the reservoir at the left end. The gas colour runs from blue for cold to red for hot.
  • PV diagram (right): the path in teal, a dashed 300 K isotherm for reference, and a shaded area for the work.
  • First-law ledger (sidebar): ΔU, Q, W, the term that is zero and the final temperature T₂.

03

The first law keeps the energy books

Heat Q is energy that flows into the gas. Work W is energy the gas gives to its surroundings by pushing the piston. Whatever is left changes the gas's internal energy U:

ΔU = Q − W
Q is positive for heat in, and W is positive for work done by the gas.

On a PV diagram the work is the area under the path, W = ∫P dV. An expansion gives positive W (teal in the sim), and a compression gives negative W (red).

Work depends on the route taken, not only on the start and end volumes. That is why the sim offers four different routes from the same starting point.

See itRun the isothermal path out to 20 L. Watch for: the teal area under the curve growing as the point moves from 1 to 2.
04

On an isothermal path ΔU = 0 and Q = W

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, U = nCVT. The 300 K reservoir holds T fixed, so ΔU = 0 and the first law leaves Q = W. Every joule of heat that flows in leaves again as work.

The path is P = nRT/V, so the area under it is

W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)

Here nRT = P₁V₁ = 1000 J, so expanding to 20 L gives W = 1000 ln 2 = 693 J. Compressing to 5 L gives −693 J. The gas is worked on, and the same 693 J of heat flows out into the reservoir.

See itRead the ledger for the isothermal path to 20 L. Watch for: ΔU = 0.00 J struck out, Q and W both 693 J, and T₂ = 300 K.
05

On an adiabatic path Q = 0 and the gas spends its own energy

With the wall insulated no heat crosses it, so Q = 0 and ΔU = −W. Expanding gas does work only by cooling. A reversible adiabat obeys PVγ = const and TVγ−1 = const, with γ = 5/3 for this monatomic gas.

Expanding from 10 L to 20 L gives T₂ = 300 × (1/2)2/3 = 189 K. Then ΔU = −555 J and W = 555 J, which is less than the 693 J of the isotherm, because no heat came in to help.

The adiabat is steeper than the isotherm through the same point. At 20 L its pressure is 0.315 bar, against 0.5 bar on the isotherm. Compressing to 5 L does the opposite: T₂ = 476 K and ΔU = +881 J.

See itRun the adiabatic path to 20 L. Watch for: Q = 0.00 J struck out, ΔU = −555 J, W = 555 J, T₂ = 189 K, and the path ending below the dashed isotherm.
06

On an isobaric path none of the three terms vanishes

At the fixed pressure of 1 bar, the work is W = PΔV. Going from 10 L to 20 L gives 10⁵ Pa × 0.010 m³ = 1000 J.

Since V ∝ T at fixed P, the gas doubles its temperature to 600 K. That raises the internal energy by ΔU = nCVΔT = (3/2)PΔV = 1500 J. The heat needed is the sum:

Q = ΔU + W = 1500 J + 1000 J = 2500 J
Q = (5/2)PΔV for a monatomic gas, so 3/5 of the heat warms the gas and 2/5 becomes work.

Compressing to 5 L gives the mirror result: T₂ = 150 K, W = −500 J, ΔU = −750 J and Q = −1250 J.

See itRun the isobaric path to 20 L. Watch for: ΔU = 1500 J, Q = 2500 J, W = 1000 J, T₂ = 600 K, and the zero term reading none.
07

On an isochoric path W = 0 and all the heat goes into U

The piston cannot move, so the path on the PV diagram is a vertical line with no area under it. Then W = 0 and the first law gives Q = ΔU = nCVΔT. Heat added raises the temperature and the pressure together, since P ∝ T at fixed V.

The sim reuses the V₂ slider as the heat knob on this path, with T₂ = 300 K × (V₂ / 10 L). The piston stays at 10 L.

  • At 20 on the slider, T₂ = 600 K, Q = ΔU = 1500 J and the pressure doubles to 2 bar.
  • At 5 on the slider the gas is cooled to 150 K, so Q = ΔU = −750 J and the pressure falls to 0.5 bar.
See itRun the isochoric path with the slider at 20. Watch for: the piston staying at 10 L, a vertical path up to 2 bar, W = 0.00 J struck out, and Q = ΔU = 1500 J.
08

Where it matters

  • Bicycle pump. A fast stroke leaves no time for heat to escape, so the compression is close to adiabatic and the air warms.
  • Diesel engine. Compressing air by a factor of 16 adiabatically takes it from 300 K to about 900 K (γ = 1.4), hot enough to ignite the fuel without a spark.
  • Slow processes. A gas that expands slowly in good thermal contact with its surroundings stays close to isothermal.
  • Rigid containers. Heating gas in a sealed can is isochoric, so the pressure rises with T and the gas does no work.
  • Heat engines. Joining several of these paths into a closed loop makes a cycle, and the net work is the area the loop encloses.
09

Summary

In one line. What a path holds fixed decides which term of ΔU = Q − W is pinned to zero, and the first law fixes the other two.

Key points

  • Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W.
  • Isobaric: none vanish, with Q = (5/2)PΔV for a monatomic gas.
  • Isochoric: W = 0, so Q = ΔU.

Common mix-ups

  • "Expanding gas always cools." The isothermal gas stays at 300 K, and the isobaric gas heats up to 600 K.
  • "Adding heat always does work." At fixed volume all the heat goes into internal energy.
  • "No heat flows in an isothermal process." The reservoir supplies exactly the heat the gas turns into work.

Things to try on your own

  • Compare W for the isothermal and adiabatic paths to 20 L, and say why one is larger.
  • Predict T₂ for the adiabatic path to 5 L, then read it from the ledger.
  • For the isobaric path to 30 L, check that Q equals (5/2)PΔV.
